title: IV. The Second Ordeal
paragraphs: "You have no idea how much you encourage us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, with your readiness to answer," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, looking animated, obvious satisfaction shining in his prominent, near-sighted, light-gray eyes, from which he'd removed his spectacles a moment before. "And your remark about mutual confidence is a very fair one — without it, it's sometimes downright impossible to get anywhere in cases of such importance, when the accused genuinely hopes and wants to defend himself and is in a position to do so. For our part, we'll do everything in our power, and you can see for yourself how we're conducting the case. You approve, Ippolit Kirillovitch?" He turned to the prosecutor.
"Oh, undoubtedly," the prosecutor replied. His tone was rather cool, compared to Nikolay Parfenovitch's enthusiasm.

I'll note, once and for all, that Nikolay Parfenovitch, who'd arrived among us only recently, had felt marked respect for Ippolit Kirillovitch, our prosecutor, from the very start, and had become almost his closest friend. He was nearly the only person who put unquestioning faith in Ippolit Kirillovitch's extraordinary gifts as a psychologist and orator, and in the justice of his grievances. He'd heard of him back in Petersburg. And, for his part, young Nikolay Parfenovitch was the one person in the whole world our "unappreciated" prosecutor genuinely liked. On the road to Mokroe they'd had time to reach an understanding about the present case. And now, sitting at the table, the sharp-witted junior man caught and read every signal from his senior colleague's face — a half-word, a glance, a wink.
"Gentlemen, just let me tell my own story and don't break in with trivial questions, and I'll tell you everything in no time," Mitya said, excitedly.

"Excellent! Thank you. But before we go on to hear your account, will you allow me to ask about one more small fact of considerable interest to us? I mean the ten roubles you borrowed yesterday, around five o'clock, against your pistols, from your friend Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin."
"I pawned them, gentlemen. Pawned them for ten roubles. What else is there to say? That's all there is to it. As soon as I got back to town, I pawned them."
"You got back to town? So you'd been out of town?"
"Yes, I went off forty versts into the countryside. Didn't you know that?"
The prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch exchanged glances.

"Well, how would it be if you began your account with a systematic description of everything you did yesterday, starting from the morning? Allow us, for instance, to ask why you were out of town, and exactly when you left and when you returned — all those facts."

"You should have asked me that way from the start," cried Mitya, laughing aloud, "and, if you like, let's not even start from yesterday, but from the morning of the day before; then you'll understand how, why, and where I went. Two days ago, gentlemen, I went to see a merchant here in town, a man named Samsonov, to borrow three thousand roubles from him against solid security. It was urgent, gentlemen, a sudden necessity."
"Allow me to interrupt," the prosecutor put in, politely. "Why were you in such urgent need of exactly that sum — three thousand?"

"Oh, gentlemen, you don't need to go into the how, the when, the why, and why exactly that much money and not some other amount, and all that rigmarole. Why, it would run to three volumes, and then you'd need an epilogue on top of it!"
Mitya said all this with the good-natured but impatient familiarity of a man eager to tell the whole truth and full of the best intentions.

"Gentlemen!" — he corrected himself hastily — "don't be annoyed at my restlessness, I ask you again. Believe me once more, I hold you in the greatest respect and understand the actual state of affairs. Don't think I'm drunk. I'm quite sober now. And besides, being drunk wouldn't be any obstacle. With me, you know, it's like the saying goes: 'Sober, he's a fool; drunk, he's a wise man.' Ha ha! But I see, gentlemen, it's not really proper to make jokes with you before we've had our talk out, I mean. And I've got my own dignity to maintain, too. I understand the difference between us perfectly well, for the moment. I am, after all, in the position of a criminal, and so, far from being your equal. And it's your job to keep an eye on me. I can't expect you to pat me on the head for what I did to Grigory, since one can't go cracking old men's skulls without consequences. I suppose you'll lock me away for that — six months, maybe a year, in a house of correction. I don't know what the sentence is — but it won't cost me my rank, my title, will it? So you see, gentlemen, I understand the distinction between us.... But you have to admit, you could confound God Himself with questions like this. 'How did you step? Where did you step? When did you step? And on what did you step?' I'll get all muddled if you keep on like this, and you'll hold it all against me. And what will that lead to? Nothing! And even if what I'm saying now is nonsense, let me finish, and you, gentlemen, being men of honor and refinement, will forgive me! Let me finish by asking you, gentlemen, to drop that standard method of questioning — I mean, starting off with some miserable trifle, how I got up, what I had for breakfast, how I spat, and where I spat, distracting the criminal's attention that way, and then suddenly hitting him with a crushing question: 'Whom did you murder? Whom did you rob?' Ha ha! That's your regulation trick, that's where all your cunning comes in. You can catch peasants off guard that way, but not me. I know the tricks. I've been in the service myself. Ha ha ha! You're not angry, gentlemen? You'll forgive my impertinence?" he cried, looking at them with a good humor that was almost startling. "It's only Mitya Karamazov, after all, so you can let it slide. It would be unforgivable in a sensible man; but you can forgive it in Mitya. Ha ha!"

Nikolay Parfenovitch listened, and laughed too. Though the prosecutor didn't laugh, he kept his eyes fixed sharply on Mitya, as though anxious not to miss the smallest syllable, the slightest movement, the tiniest twitch of a feature.

"That's exactly how we've treated you from the start," said Nikolay Parfenovitch, still laughing. "We haven't tried to throw you off by asking how you got up in the morning or what you had for breakfast. We began, in fact, with the most important questions."

"I understand. I noticed it and appreciated it, and I appreciate your kindness to me now even more, an unprecedented kindness, worthy of your noble hearts. The three of us here are gentlemen, so let everything proceed on a footing of mutual trust, between educated, well-bred people, bound together by the common ties of noble birth and honor. In any case, allow me to regard you as my best friends at this moment in my life — this moment when my honor is under attack. That's no offense to you, gentlemen, is it?"
"Quite the opposite. You've put that beautifully, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Nikolay Parfenovitch answered, with dignified approval.
"And enough of those trivial questions, gentlemen, all those tricky little questions!" Mitya cried, enthusiastically. "Or there'll simply be no telling where we'll end up! Isn't that so?"

"I'll follow your sensible advice entirely," the prosecutor put in, addressing Mitya. "I don't withdraw my question, though. It's now vitally important for us to know exactly why you needed that sum — precisely three thousand."
"Why I needed it?... Oh, this and that.... Well, it was to pay off a debt."
"A debt to whom?"

"That I flatly refuse to answer, gentlemen. Not because I couldn't, or wouldn't dare, or because it would harm me, since it's really a paltry, thoroughly trivial matter — but I won't, on principle: that's my private life, and I won't allow anyone to intrude on my private life. That's my principle. Your question has no bearing on the case, and whatever has nothing to do with the case is my own affair. I wanted to pay a debt. A debt of honor. But to whom, I won't say."
"Allow me to note that down," said the prosecutor.
"By all means. Write down that I won't say, that I won't. Write that I'd consider it dishonorable to say. Ech, go ahead and write it; you've got nothing better to do with your time."

"Allow me to caution you, sir, and remind you once more, in case you're unaware," the prosecutor began, with a peculiar, stern weight, "that you have every right not to answer the questions put to you now, and that we, for our part, have no right to force an answer out of you if you decline to give one, for whatever reason. That's entirely your own decision to make. But it is our duty, on the other hand, in cases like this one, to explain and lay before you just how much harm you'll do yourself by refusing to give this or that piece of testimony. After which I'll ask you to continue."
"Gentlemen, I'm not angry ... I ..." Mitya muttered, in a rather flustered tone. "Well, gentlemen, you see, that Samsonov I went to see then ..."

We won't, of course, reproduce his account of what the reader already knows. Mitya was impatiently anxious not to leave out the smallest detail. At the same time, he was in a hurry to get it over with. But since his testimony was being written down as he gave it, they had to keep interrupting him. Mitya disliked this, but put up with it; he grew irritated, though still good-humoredly. He did, it's true, exclaim now and then, "Gentlemen, that's enough to try an angel's patience!" Or, "Gentlemen, it does you no good to irritate me."

But even with these exclamations, he kept up, for a time, his genially expansive mood. So he told them how Samsonov had made a fool of him two days before. (He'd fully realized by now that he'd been fooled.) The lawyers found the sale of his watch for six roubles, to raise money for the trip, entirely new to them. It interested them at once, and, to Mitya's intense indignation, they even thought it necessary to write it down as secondary confirmation that he'd been all but penniless at the time. Little by little Mitya began growing surly. Then, having described his trip to see Lyagavy, the night spent in the stifling hut, and so on, he arrived at his return to town. Here, without being pressed, he began giving a minute account of the agonies of jealousy he'd suffered over Grushenka.

He was heard out in silent attention. They asked particularly about his having a lookout post at Marya Kondratyevna's house, behind Fyodor Pavlovitch's garden, to keep watch on Grushenka, and about Smerdyakov bringing him information. They laid special stress on this point, and noted it down. He spoke of his jealousy warmly and at length, and though inwardly ashamed to be exposing his most intimate feelings to "public disgrace," so to speak, he evidently overcame his shame in order to tell the truth. The cold severity with which the investigating lawyer, and even more the prosecutor, stared intently at him as he told his story eventually left him considerably unsettled.

"That boy, Nikolay Parfenovitch, to whom I was talking nonsense about women only a few days ago, and that sickly prosecutor — they're not worth telling this to," he reflected, mournfully. "It's disgraceful. 'Be patient, be humble, hold thy peace.'" He closed his thoughts with that line. But he pulled himself together and went on. When he got to his visit to Madame Hohlakov, his spirits picked up, and he even tried to tell a little anecdote about the lady that had nothing to do with the case. But the investigating lawyer stopped him, and politely suggested he move on to "more essential matters." At last, when he described his despair, and told them how, on leaving Madame Hohlakov's, he'd thought he'd "get three thousand if he had to kill someone to do it," they stopped him again and noted down that he'd "intended to kill someone." Mitya let them write it without protest. At last he reached the point in his story where he learned that Grushenka had deceived him, and had left Samsonov's the moment he departed, though she'd told him she'd stay there until midnight.

"If I didn't kill Fenya right then, gentlemen, it was only because I didn't have time," burst out of him suddenly, at that point in his story. That, too, was carefully written down. Mitya waited, gloomy, and was starting to tell how he'd run into his father's garden when the investigating lawyer suddenly stopped him, and, opening the large portfolio lying on the sofa beside him, brought out the brass pestle.
"Do you recognize this object?" he asked, showing it to Mitya.
"Oh, yes," he laughed, gloomily. "Of course I recognize it. Let me have a look.... Damn it, never mind!"
"You forgot to mention it," the investigating lawyer observed.
"Hang it all, I wouldn't have hidden it from you. Do you think I could have managed without it? It just slipped my mind."
"Would you be so good as to tell us exactly how you came to arm yourself with it?"
"Certainly I'll be so good, gentlemen."
And Mitya described how he'd grabbed the pestle and run.
"But what was your purpose in arming yourself with such a weapon?"
"Purpose? No purpose at all. I just grabbed it and ran off."
"What for, then, if you had no purpose?"

Mitya's temper flared. He looked hard at "the boy" and smiled, gloomy and malicious. He was growing more and more ashamed of having told "people like this" the story of his jealousy so sincerely, so openly.
"To hell with the pestle!" burst from him suddenly.
"But even so—"
"Oh, to keep off dogs.... Oh, because it was dark.... In case something came up."
"But have you ever, on other occasions, taken a weapon with you when going out, given that you're afraid of the dark?"

"Ugh, damn it all, gentlemen! There's simply no talking to you people!" cried Mitya, pushed past endurance, and, turning to the secretary, crimson with anger, he said quickly, a note of fury in his voice:

"Write down right now ... right now ... 'that I snatched up the pestle to go and kill my father ... Fyodor Pavlovitch ... by striking him on the head with it!' Well, are you satisfied now, gentlemen? Does that put your minds at ease?" he said, glaring defiantly at the two lawyers.

"We understand perfectly well that you made that statement just now out of exasperation at us, and at the questions we've been asking, which you consider trivial, even though they're actually essential," the prosecutor remarked, dryly, in reply.

"Well, upon my word, gentlemen! Yes, I took the pestle.... What does a man pick things up for, at moments like that? I don't know what for. I grabbed it and ran — that's all. As for why, gentlemen, passons — let's drop it, or I swear I won't tell you another word."

He sat with his elbows on the table and his head in his hand. He sat turned sideways to them, staring at the wall, fighting off a wave of nausea. He genuinely felt a terrible urge to stand up and declare that he wouldn't say another word, "not if you hang me for it."

"You see, gentlemen," he said at last, struggling to control himself, "you see. I listen to you, and I'm haunted by a dream.... It's a dream I have sometimes, you know.... I dream it often — always the same one ... that someone is hunting me, someone I'm terribly afraid of ... that he's hunting me in the dark, at night ... tracking me, and I hide somewhere from him, behind a door or a cupboard, hiding in some degrading way, and the worst part is, he always knows exactly where I am, but pretends not to know on purpose, just to drag out my agony, to enjoy my terror.... That's exactly what you're doing right now. It's exactly like that!"
"Is that the kind of thing you dream about?" the prosecutor asked.
"Yes, it is. Don't you want to write it down?" said Mitya, with a twisted smile.
"No, no need to write that down. But you do have some curious dreams, all the same."
"It's not a matter of dreams now, gentlemen — this is realism, this is real life! I'm a wolf, and you're the hunters. Well, hunt him down, then!"
"You're wrong to make such comparisons ..." Nikolay Parfenovitch began, with extraordinary gentleness.

"No, I'm not wrong, not in the least!" Mitya flared up again, though his outburst had clearly eased his heart. He grew more good-humored with every word. "You may not trust a criminal, or a man on trial, worn down by your questions — but an honorable man, the honorable impulses of his heart — I say that boldly! — no, that you have no right to distrust ... but—
Be silent, heart, Be patient, be humble, hold thy peace.
Well, shall I go on?" he broke off, gloomily.
"If you would be so kind," answered Nikolay Parfenovitch.
